title: Chapter 16 — The Effect Of Democracy On Language
paragraphs: If the reader has rightly grasped what I have already said about literature in general, he will have no difficulty in understanding the kind of influence a democratic social condition and democratic institutions can exercise over language itself, which is the chief instrument of thought.

American authors can truly be said to live more in England than in their own country, since they constantly study the English writers and take them every day as their models. But this is not the case with the bulk of the population, which is more directly subject to the particular causes at work in the United States. It is therefore not to the written but to the spoken language that attention must be paid, if we wish to detect the changes the idiom of an aristocratic people undergoes when it becomes the language of a democracy.

Educated Englishmen — more competent judges than I can be of the finer shades of expression — have often assured me that the language of the educated classes in the United States is noticeably different from that of the educated classes in Great Britain. They complain not only that the Americans have brought into use a number of new words — the difference and the distance between the two countries might be enough to explain that much — but that these new words are especially drawn from the jargon of parties, the mechanical arts, or the language of trade. They add that old English words are often used by the Americans in new senses. And lastly, that the inhabitants of the United States frequently mix their phrasing in the strangest way, sometimes placing together words that are always kept apart in the language of the mother country. These remarks, made to me at various times by persons who seemed worthy of credit, led me to reflect on the subject; and my reflections brought me, by theoretical reasoning, to the same point my informants had reached through practical observation.

In aristocracies, language naturally shares in that state of repose in which everything stays put. Few new words are coined because few new things are made; and even if new things were made, they would be called by known words whose meanings have been fixed by tradition. If the human mind does at last stir itself, or is roused by light breaking in from outside, the new expressions introduced bear a stamp of learning, intelligence, and philosophy that shows they do not originate in a democracy. After the fall of Constantinople turned the tide of science and literature toward the west, the French language was almost immediately invaded by a multitude of new words, all with Greek or Latin roots. An erudite neologism then sprang up in France, confined to the educated classes and producing no noticeable effect on the people, or at most a very gradual one. All the nations of Europe in turn exhibited the same change. Milton alone introduced more than six hundred words into the English language, almost all drawn from Latin, Greek, or Hebrew. The constant agitation that prevails in a democratic community tends, by contrast, ceaselessly to change the character of the language, just as it changes the look of affairs. Amid this general stir and competition of minds, a great number of new ideas are formed, and old ideas are lost, or reappear, or are subdivided into an infinite variety of minor shades. The result is that many words must fall out of use and others must be brought into it.

Democratic nations love change for its own sake, and this is as visible in their language as in their politics. Even when they have no need to change words, they sometimes feel a wish to transform them. The genius of a democratic people shows itself not only in the great number of words it puts into circulation, but in the nature of the ideas those new words represent. Among such a people the majority makes the law in language, as it does in everything else, and its prevailing spirit is as evident in that as in other respects. But the majority is more occupied with business than with study, with political and commercial interests than with philosophical speculation or literary pursuits. Most of the words coined or adopted for its use will therefore bear the mark of these habits; they will mostly serve to express the needs of business, the passions of party, or the details of public administration. In these areas the language will constantly spread, while on the other hand it will gradually lose ground in metaphysics and theology.

As to the source from which democratic nations usually draw their new expressions, and the way they go about coining them, both can easily be described. Men living in democratic countries know little of the language spoken at Athens or Rome, and they do not care to dive into the lore of antiquity to find the expression they happen to want. If they sometimes resort to learned etymologies, vanity will lead them to search at the roots of the dead languages, but erudition does not naturally supply them with its resources. It sometimes happens that the most ignorant make the most use of them. The eminently democratic desire to rise above one's own sphere will often lead men to dignify a common profession with a Greek or Latin name. The lower the calling, and the further from learning, the more pompous and erudite its name. Thus French rope-dancers have transformed themselves into acrobates and funambules.

In the absence of knowledge of the dead languages, democratic nations are apt to borrow words from living tongues; for their mutual dealings become perpetual, and the inhabitants of different countries imitate each other the more readily as they grow more alike every day.

But it is chiefly on their own languages that democratic nations attempt innovations. From time to time they revive forgotten expressions from their vocabulary and bring them back into use, or they borrow from some particular class of the community a term peculiar to it and introduce it with a figurative meaning into the language of daily life. Many expressions that originally belonged to the technical language of a profession or a party are drawn in this way into general circulation.

The most common expedient by which democratic nations introduce innovations into language is to give an unusual meaning to an expression already in use. This method is very simple, quick, and convenient. No learning is required to use it correctly, and ignorance itself rather helps the practice. But that practice is most dangerous to the language. When a democratic people doubles the meaning of a word in this way, it sometimes leaves the meaning it keeps as ambiguous as the one it acquires. An author begins with a slight deflection of a known expression from its original meaning and adapts it, thus modified, as best he can to his subject. A second writer twists the sense of the expression in another way; a third takes possession of it for another purpose. Since there is no common appeal to the verdict of a permanent tribunal that could definitively settle the meaning of the word, it remains in an ambiguous state. The result is that writers hardly ever seem to dwell on a single thought; they always seem to aim at a cluster of ideas, leaving the reader to judge which of them has been hit. This is a deplorable consequence of democracy. I would rather that the language should be made hideous with words imported from the Chinese, the Tartars, or the Hurons than that the meaning of a word in our own language should become indeterminate. Harmony and uniformity are only secondary beauties in composition; many of these things are conventional, and strictly speaking they can be done without. But without clear phrasing there is no good language.

The principle of equality necessarily introduces several other changes into language. In aristocratic ages, when each nation tends to stand apart from all others and likes to have distinct characteristics of its own, it often happens that several peoples with a common origin nevertheless become estranged from one another, so that, without ceasing to understand the same language, they no longer all speak it in the same way. In these ages each nation is divided into a certain number of classes that see little of each other and do not mingle. Each of these classes contracts, and invariably keeps, habits of mind peculiar to itself, and chooses certain words and terms that are afterwards handed down from generation to generation, like their estates. The same idiom then includes a language of the poor and a language of the rich — a language of the citizen and a language of the nobility, a learned language and a vulgar one. The deeper the divisions and the more impassable the barriers of society become, the more this must be the case. I would lay a wager that among the castes of India there are astonishing variations of language, and that there is almost as much difference between the language of the pariah and that of the Brahmin as there is in their dress. By contrast, when men, no longer restrained by ranks, meet in constant contact — when castes are destroyed and the classes of society recruit and blend with each other — all the words of a language are mingled. Those unsuitable to the greater number die out; the rest form a common store from which everyone draws almost at random. Nearly all the different dialects that once divided the idioms of European nations are visibly declining; there is no patois in the New World, and it is disappearing every day from the old countries.

The influence of this revolution in social conditions is felt in style as much as in phrasing. Not only does everyone use the same words, but a habit springs up of using them without discrimination. The rules style had set up are almost abolished. The line ceases to be drawn between expressions that seem by their very nature common and others that appear refined. People coming from different ranks of society carry the terms and expressions they are used to with them into whatever circles they move in. The origin of words is thus lost, like the origin of individuals, and there is as much confusion in language as there is in society.

I am aware that in the classification of words there are rules that do not belong to one form of society more than to another, but are drawn from the nature of things. Some expressions and phrases are vulgar because the ideas they are meant to express are low in themselves; others are of a higher character because the objects they are meant to designate are naturally elevated. No intermixture of ranks will ever erase these differences. But the principle of equality cannot fail to root out whatever is merely conventional and arbitrary in the forms of thought. Perhaps the necessary classification I have just pointed out will always be less respected by a democratic people than by any other, because among such a people there are no men permanently disposed by education, culture, and leisure to study the natural laws of language and to cause those laws to be respected by observing them themselves.

I will not leave this topic without touching on a feature of democratic languages that is perhaps more characteristic of them than any other. It has already been shown that democratic nations have a taste, and sometimes a passion, for general ideas, and that this arises from their peculiar merits and defects. This liking for general ideas shows itself in democratic languages in the continual use of generic terms and abstract expressions, and in the way they are used. This is the great merit and the great defect of these languages. Democratic nations are passionately addicted to generic terms and abstract expressions because such modes of speech enlarge thought and assist the operations of the mind by enabling it to include several objects in a small compass. A French democratic writer will be apt to say capacités in the abstract for men of capacity, without specifying the objects to which their capacity is applied. He will speak of actualités to designate in a single word the things happening before his eyes at that moment, and he will take in under the term éventualités whatever may happen in the universe from the moment he is speaking. Democratic writers are perpetually coining words of this kind, in which they sublimate into further abstraction the already abstract terms of the language. More than that, to make their mode of speech more concise, they personify the subject of these abstract terms and make it act as a real entity. Thus they will say in French: "La force des choses veut que les capacités gouvernent."

I cannot better illustrate what I mean than by my own example. I have often used the word "equality" in an absolute sense; indeed I have personified equality in several places. Thus I have said that equality does such and such things, or refrains from doing others. It may be said that the writers of the age of Louis XIV would not have used such expressions. They would never have thought of using the word "equality" without applying it to some particular object, and they would rather have given up the term altogether than consent to turn it into a living personage.

These abstract terms, which abound in democratic languages and are used on every occasion without being attached to any particular fact, enlarge and obscure the thoughts they are meant to convey. They make the mode of speech more concise and the idea in it less clear. But where language is concerned, democratic nations prefer obscurity to labor. I do not know whether this loose style has some secret charm for those who speak and write among these nations. Since the men who live there are often thrown back on the efforts of their individual minds, they are almost always prey to doubt. And since their situation in life is forever changing, they are never held fast to any of their opinions by the secure tenure of their fortunes. Men living in democratic countries are therefore apt to have unsettled ideas, and they need loose expressions to convey them. Since they never know whether the idea they express today will be appropriate to the new position they may occupy tomorrow, they naturally develop a liking for abstract terms. An abstract term is like a box with a false bottom: you can put in it whatever ideas you please and take them out again without being observed.

Among all nations, generic and abstract terms form the basis of language. I do not, then, pretend to banish these terms from democratic languages. I simply note that men have a special tendency, in the ages of democracy, to multiply words of this kind — to take them always by themselves in their most abstract sense, and to use them on every occasion, even when the nature of the discourse does not call for them.
